paras: The Charley Hudson peonage case was a 1903 federal prosecution in Birmingham, Alabama, of members of the Dill family of Lamar County, accused of seizing Hudson, a Black man, on a public road, working him without pay, and having him whipped after he tried to escape. In November 1903 Marshall and Archie Dill were each fined $400, and the case against their father, Aaron Dill, was dropped. Papers outside Alabama carried the hearing testimony as a "flagrant case" and an instance of "modern slavery."

Secret Service Agent J. M. Wright swore that on August 27, 1903, Aaron Dill, Archie Dill and Marcellus Lockhart seized "Charley Hutson" from the highway and held him in involuntary servitude, and charged each with peonage and conspiracy. A deputy marshal arrested the three near Guin in Marion County on September 22, though later reports placed the Dill farm and the offenses in Lamar County. Bob Stevenson, a Black laborer on the farm and the government's principal witness, was himself held on the same charges.

At the hearing of Aaron and Archie Dill on September 25, testimony showed that Hudson was stopped on the road near the Dill place and put to cutting railroad ties for Marshall Dill. He testified that he was locked at night in a cotton house and that, after an escape, he was caught two miles down the road and given "ninety lashes with a hickory stick" until his shirt was wet with blood. He was never paid, he said, and Dill took his clothing and $10; other testimony told of his being beaten over the head and having guns pointed at him and snapped.

Stevenson, who said he had contracted with Dill for $9 a month and been leased to Lockhart, testified that Dill snapped both barrels of a shotgun at the fleeing Hudson without effect. Once caught, Hudson was tied and marched home, where Archie Dill knocked him down, and Stevenson whipped him at a tree while Marshall Dill held a pistol on him. Two white witnesses supported the account: farmer C. A. Booker saw Dill wearing Hudson's pants and shoes, and miller Ed Knight said Dill had brought Hudson, with a gash in his head, to his mill and said, "I want to sell you this negro; I am going to Mississippi."

The defense did not deny that the law had been broken but called Marshall Dill the chief offender, and Commissioner A. C. Birch bound Aaron and Archie Dill over to the grand jury under $1,500 bond each. Marshall Dill was captured near Amory, Mississippi, by Deputy Marshal J. D. Dennis, waived examination on September 29, and was held under $2,000 bond on each charge. On October 9 the commissioner dismissed Lockhart, and Aaron Dill was released on bond.

In the U.S. court on November 25 the case against Aaron Dill was nol prossed and Marshall and Archie Dill were each fined $400. The notice did not say whether they pleaded guilty or were convicted, and no report of the charges against Stevenson or a fourth defendant, Lee Crump, was found.

The Birmingham Age-Herald covered the case most fully, promising testimony "the most sensational heard in the court for many a day" and heading its hearing report "Negroes Imprisoned and Flogged." It introduced Marshall Dill as an "alleged keeper of peons, alleged conspirator and alleged all round bad man," while the Montgomery Advertiser followed the hearings in more procedural terms.

The Associated Press dispatch ran in the Louisville Courier-Journal as "Flagrant case if this negro tells truth about his treatment" and in the Raleigh News & Observer as "Brutal Treatment of a Negro Shown," with shorter versions in Savannah and Indianapolis. Weekly digests in Michigan, South Dakota and Florida carried a sentence or two into October, citing "modern slavery in Alabama" and "horrible brutality." All of this coverage appeared in white papers; no report of the case was found in the Black press.

The affidavit named Aaron and Archie Dill and Lockhart as Hudson's captors, while Hudson and Stevenson named Marshall Dill, and the wire report had Marshall Dill do the whipping that Stevenson said he performed under Dill's pistol.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Marshall Dill, aided by Stevenson, pursued and caught Hudson and whipped him tied to a tree; he was beaten, knocked down and had guns pointed at him and snapped.

accounts.label: Defense argument

framing.detail: The Birmingham Age-Herald headlined 'Negroes Imprisoned and Flogged' and called Marshall Dill an 'alleged all round bad man' and 'the worst one of the whole gang'.
The Montgomery Advertiser's Birmingham reports followed each hearing in a procedural tone ('Peonage in Lamar County', 'Another Arrest Made').
The AP dispatch ran as 'Flagrant case if this negro tells truth', 'Brutal Treatment of a Negro Shown' and 'Farmers Charged With Peonage'.
Northern weekly digests called it 'modern slavery in Alabama' and 'horrible brutality'.

conflicts.note: Arrests near Guin were reported in Marion County, but hearing testimony and later reports place the Dill farm and the offenses in Lamar County; the later, testimony-based reports are the better evidence for the site.
